q: The luminosity of a star is:
o: The power received per square metre at the Earth
The total power it radiates in all directions
Its surface temperature
Its distance from the Earth
x: Luminosity L is the total energy a star radiates per second, measured in watts. The power received per square metre at a distance d is the radiant flux F = L/(4πd²), which depends on distance as well.

q: The radiant flux from the Sun at the Earth is 1.4 × 10³ W m⁻² and the Earth-Sun distance is 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. Using F = L/(4πd²) with π ≈ 3.14, the luminosity of the Sun is about:
o: 1 × 10²⁶ W
4 × 10²⁶ W
x: L = 4πd²F = 4 × 3.14 × (1.5 × 10¹¹)² × 1.4 × 10³ = 12.56 × 2.25 × 10²² × 1.4 × 10³ ≈ 4 × 10²⁶ W. Leaving out the 4 gives 1 × 10²⁶ W; leaving out 4π gives 3.2 × 10²⁵ W; forgetting to square d gives 2.6 × 10¹⁵ W.

q: According to Hubble's law v = H₀d, with H₀ the Hubble constant, a rough estimate of the age of the universe is given by:
o: 1/H₀
H₀
H₀²
H₀ × c
x: If galaxies have been moving apart at steady speeds, a galaxy at distance d took time d/v = d/(H₀d) = 1/H₀ to get there, so 1/H₀ estimates the age. A larger H₀ would mean a younger universe.

q: Astronomers on the Earth see distant galaxies moving away in every direction, faster the farther away they are. This means that:
o: The Earth is at the centre of the expansion
The galaxies are moving through a fixed space away from our Galaxy only
Galaxies nearer to us must be moving faster
Observers in any galaxy would see the same pattern, so the Earth is not at a centre
x: In a uniform expansion (v = H₀d) every distance grows in the same proportion, so from any galaxy all others appear to recede with speed proportional to distance; there is no centre. Nearer galaxies recede more slowly, not faster.

q: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour warm the Earth's surface because they:
o: Let most incoming sunlight through but absorb and re-emit the infrared radiation given off by the Earth
Absorb all the incoming sunlight before it reaches the ground
Reflect sunlight back into space
Produce heat by chemical reactions in the air
x: Sunlight (mostly visible, short wavelength) passes through and warms the ground; the warm ground radiates infrared, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate partly back down, so less heat escapes. Reflecting sunlight would cool the Earth, not warm it.

q: Warm surface ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream flow from the tropics towards higher latitudes. Their main effect on climate is to:
o: Carry heat from the poles to the equator
Carry heat from low latitudes to high latitudes, making nearby coasts milder
Stop the atmosphere from circulating
Make the coasts they pass much colder in winter
x: Ocean currents transport large amounts of heat; warm currents moving poleward release it at higher latitudes, which is why north-western Europe is milder than other places at the same latitude. Cold currents do the reverse, flowing towards the equator.
